pages.markdown: Horizontal bar chart ranking positive attributes reported by recreational anglers in the United States. Getting away from the usual demands leads at 34%, followed by being close to nature (33%), enjoying the sounds and smells of nature (32%), and catching fish (31%). Spending time with family or friends is 29%; scenic beauty is 16%; experiencing solitude and excitement/adventure are tied at 14%; and reliving childhood memories of going fishing and catching one’s own food are tied at 12%. Figure 10.2: Positive attributes reported by recreational anglers in the United States. Long description. Over time, an angler’s motivation may change from a catch orientation to emphasize noncatch motivations, such as being outdoors or passing on their passion for fishing (McKenna 2013). The progression often follows these stages: • Stage 1: I just want to catch a fish! • Stage 2: I want to catch a lot of fish! • Stage 3: I want to catch big fish. • Stage 4: I’m just happy to be out fishing. • Stage 5: I want to pass on my knowledge and passion for fishing. Studies of angler characteristics confirm that there is no such thing as an “average” angler. Rather, anglers are a heterogeneous and changing group. Therefore, we can segment anglers in distinct categories for analysis (Bryan 1977; Kyle et al. 2007; Beardmore et al. 2013; TenHarmsel et al. 2019). For example, Magee (2018) categorized recreational anglers into five distinct fisher classes with differing motivations (Table 10.1). 216 | Recreational Fishing and Keep Fish Wet
